title: Bitwise ORs of Subarrays
description: Brute force to optimized: computing every subarray's OR directly versus a Kadane's-style bounded set tracking, exploiting OR's monotonicity.

blocks.text: Given an integer array arr, return the number of distinct values achievable as the bitwise OR of some non-empty contiguous subarray of arr.

blocks.caption: Track a set of OR values ending at each position, not just a single running value

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An integer array arr"],["Output","The count of distinct bitwise-OR values achievable across all non-empty contiguous subarrays of arr"],["Goal","Find this without literally computing and storing every possible subarray's OR value"],["Constraints","1 <= arr.length <= 5 * 10^4; 0 <= arr[i] <= 10^9"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Looking for the count of DISTINCT values across all subarrays, not a single maximum","Kadane's \"extend or restart\" recurrence, generalized from a single running value to a SET of running values"],["Bitwise OR only ever SETS bits, never clears them","The number of distinct values ending at any position is naturally bounded by the number of bits (about 30 for typical constraints), keeping the tracked set small"],["The set of OR values ending at position i is built directly from the set ending at position i-1","Extend every previous value with the current element (via OR), plus include the current element alone as a fresh start"]]}

blocks.text: Given an integer array arr, count how many distinct values can be produced by taking the bitwise OR of some non-empty contiguous subarray.

blocks.title: Analogy: Every Way to Combine a Row of Colored Light Filters
blocks.text: Like having a row of light filters, each letting through a fixed combination of colors, and wanting to know every distinct combination of colors achievable by stacking any contiguous run of filters together (stacking only ever adds more colors through, never removes any, since each filter's colors OR together). Rather than testing every possible stretch of filters individually, tracking only the combinations achievable ending at each position (and how they build directly from the position before) is enough, since stacking on one more filter can only grow, never shrink, the set of colors let through.

blocks.caption: A value can only gain bits as it grows, bounding how many distinct values can ever end at one position

Ending at index 2: {4, 2|4=6, 3|4=7}","Distinct values overall: {1,2,3,4,6,7}","Every one of these values is achievable by some contiguous subarray"],["Answer","6","There are 6 distinct achievable OR values across every subarray of arr"]]}

blocks.text: Before computing every subarray's OR value individually, notice this is Kadane's "extend or restart" idea, but tracking a whole SET of possibilities ending at each position instead of just one.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The set of achievable OR values for subarrays ENDING exactly at position i can be built directly from the set ending at position i-1: take every value in that previous set, OR it with arr[i], and also include arr[i] alone (the subarray starting fresh at position i).

Observation 2: This mirrors Kadane's single-value "extend or restart" recurrence exactly, generalized to track a SET of "best" (here, all distinct achievable) values instead of just one.

Observation 3: Since OR only ever adds bits and never removes them, the set of distinct values ending at any single position can never exceed the number of bits in the values involved (about 30 for typical 32-bit integers), keeping each position's set small regardless of how large arr is.

Observation 4: Union every position's set of ending values into one overall result set across the whole array, and the answer is simply that result set's size.

Recognizing that "OR is monotonic" bounds the set size is the key insight that keeps this approach efficient, turning an apparently exponential search into a near-linear one.

This is Kadane's Algorithm generalized from tracking a single running value to tracking a bounded SET of running values, exploiting that bitwise OR only ever grows (never shrinks) as more elements are included.
For every possible starting index, extend forward one element at a time, OR-ing in each new element and recording every distinct value seen.

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward, maintaining a running OR value.
Add every intermediate OR value encountered to a global set of seen values.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh running OR value is used for every starting position, since each independent walk accumulates its own subarray OR.
seen naturally deduplicates every distinct value encountered, across every starting position and extension.
The |= operator is used directly, since OR-ing a value into itself repeatedly correctly accumulates the running subarray OR.

blocks.text: Every possible subarray's OR value is computed directly, so every distinct achievable value is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each of the n starting positions walks forward up to n elements.
Space: O(n squared) in the worst case, for storing every intermediate value seen.

Limitation: restarting the running OR from scratch at every new starting position ignores that the set of achievable values ending at any position can be built directly and compactly from the set ending at the position right before it.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force restarts its running OR value from scratch at every starting position. Instead, maintain current, the SET of distinct OR values achievable by subarrays ending exactly at the current position. At each step, build the new current set from the previous one: OR every previous value with the new element, and also add the new element alone (a fresh start). Since OR only ever sets bits, this set never grows beyond around 30 distinct values, keeping the whole pass efficient. Union every position's current set into an overall result set, and return its size.

Maintain a set current, representing every distinct OR value achievable ending at the current position, and a set result, accumulating every distinct value seen anywhere. At each element x, build the new current as {x} unioned with {prev | x for every prev in the old current}, then merge current into result.
Track a small, bounded set of OR values ending at each position, built directly from the previous position's set.

blocks.content: {"headers":["x","New current = {x} union {prev|x for prev in old current}","result so far"],"rows":[["1","{1} (old current was empty)","{1}"],["2","{2} union {1|2=3} = {2, 3}","{1, 2, 3}"],["4","{4} union {2|4=6, 3|4=7} = {4, 6, 7}","{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7}"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The overall result set has 6 distinct values: {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7}, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * 30) which simplifies to O(n), since each position's set holds at most about 30 distinct values (bounded by the bit width), and building the next set costs O(30) work.
Space: O(n * 30) for the result set in the worst case (still effectively linear).

Every subarray ending at position i either starts fresh at i (contributing just arr[i] to the set) or extends some subarray ending at position i-1 (contributing prev | arr[i] for each such prev). Since OR-ing never removes a bit once set, repeated OR operations can only ever increase (or leave unchanged) a value, which caps how many distinct values can possibly exist in any one position's set: at most as many as the number of bits, since each additional distinct value must differ by at least one newly-set bit along some chain of extensions.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Building the new \"current\" set","Union of {the current element alone} and {every previous ending value OR-ed with the current element}"],["Merging into \"result\"","Every value in the new current set is added to the overall running result set"]]}

items: current is completely rebuilt at each step, since every subarray ending at the previous position could still extend into the current one.
The current element alone is always included, representing a subarray that starts fresh at this position.
result accumulates values across the ENTIRE array's history, while current only ever reflects the most recent position.

blocks.text: This problem generalizes Kadane's Algorithm from tracking a single running value to tracking a small, BOUNDED set of running values, made efficient specifically because bitwise OR is monotonic (only ever sets bits, never clears them).

items: Not realizing the "current" set stays small (bounded by bit-width) and instead fearing the algorithm might blow up in size, leading to an unnecessarily complicated alternative approach.
Forgetting to include the current element alone (a fresh start) when building the new current set, missing subarrays that begin exactly at the current position.
Confusing "current" (values ending exactly here) with "result" (all values seen anywhere so far); only current needs to be rebuilt each step, while result simply accumulates.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["arr has only 1 element","The answer is always 1, since that single element is the only possible subarray"],["arr is entirely zeros","The answer is 1, since every subarray's OR value is 0"],["arr has many repeated identical values","The set of distinct OR values may end up quite small, since repeating an OR with the same value never changes it"]]}

items: Explicitly justify WHY tracking a set instead of a single value stays efficient here (the monotonic, bit-setting nature of OR bounds the set size), since this justification is the crux of why the approach works at all.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count distinct values achievable by some monotonic combining operation (OR, AND, GCD) over all subarrays" points toward Kadane's-style tracking of a bounded SET of values ending at each position, exploiting the operation's monotonicity to keep that set small.

items: Would this same technique work for bitwise AND instead of OR? Yes, AND is also monotonic (only ever clears bits), so the same bounded-set technique applies directly, just swapping OR for AND in the recurrence.

Would this technique work for addition instead of OR? No, addition is not bit-bounded in the same way; the set of achievable sums ending at any position could grow much larger, since there's no equivalent "at most 30 distinct values" guarantee.

How would you find the actual subarrays achieving a specific OR value, not just count distinct values? Additional bookkeeping (e.g., tracking one representative starting index per achievable value at each position) would be needed alongside the value itself.

A generalization of Kadane's Algorithm from a single running value to a small, bounded set of running values, made tractable by exploiting the monotonicity of the OR operation, in the same broad family as Maximum Subarray and Longest Continuous Increasing Subsequence.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n squared) space.
Optimized (Kadane's-style bounded set tracking): O(n * bit-width) time and space, effectively O(n).

items: Pattern: Kadane's-style tracking of a bounded SET of values ending at each position, instead of a single running value
Core Idea: The set of OR values ending at position i extends every value from position i-1 (via OR) plus the current element alone; OR's monotonicity keeps this set small
Time: O(n) (technically O(n * bit-width))
Space: O(n) (technically O(n * bit-width))
Most Important Observation: Bitwise OR only ever sets bits, never clears them, bounding how many distinct values can end at any single position
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Track a small set of "OR values ending here"; extend each with the new element, plus the element alone
